title: The patriarchs in their world
titleTurn: Abraham to Joseph, among the tablets
premise: Genesis 12 to 50 tells of four generations of one family who move between Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt. Thousands of tablets and inscriptions from those lands show names, family customs, contracts and court life like the ones in these chapters. A likeness can show that a story fits a world. It cannot, by itself, fix the story's date, and it cannot tell us whether a named person lived. This study lays out what each likeness can carry and what it cannot.
question: When a custom in Genesis matches a tablet, what does the match actually date: the people, the writing, or nothing at all?
outcomes: Name the main kinds of outside evidence set beside Genesis 12–50: names, places, family law, contracts, and pictures of travellers.
For any parallel, ask how long the custom lasted. A custom found across fifteen centuries cannot date a story to one of them.
Explain why the same Nuzi tablets were read as proof in the 1950s and set aside in the 1970s, and what the evidence itself never changed.
Test four popular claims (the camels, the Philistines, Ebla, the Hyksos) and say which conclusion the sources support and which they do not.
Tell a reconstruction of the patriarchs' dates from a correction of the text, and say why this site does not choose between the placements.

boundaries.in: Genesis 12–50 set beside written and pictured evidence from Mesopotamia, Syria, Canaan and Egypt, mainly from about 2000 to 1200 BC, with later evidence wherever the argument needs it.
out: Genesis 1–11, the flood and the tablets of Mesopotamia that tell of one: Genesis 1–11: the questions readers bring (50) and its own planned academic study take them.

The covenant with Abraham as teaching, including Genesis 12:1–7 and 15: Covenants and promises (26) owns those passages. This page only asks how the covenant ceremonies look beside ancient treaties, and walks no passage.
Sarah, Hagar, Rebekah, Leah, Rachel and Tamar as people of faith: Women of the Bible (46). Here they appear only where a custom touches them.
The exodus, its date and the Habiru: the planned study of the exodus and settlement. Egypt beside Israel (32) already reads the Amarna letters and tests the Habiru claim.
Egypt's later dealings with Judah: Israel among the empires.
Whether the patriarchs believed in one God, and how their faith grew: Knowing God (21). This page compares worlds, not doctrines.

figures.label: Chapters
figures.caption: Genesis 12 to 50, Abraham's call to Joseph's coffin, all set beside outside evidence

figures.label: Records
figures.caption: Each one in three parts: what the evidence says, what the study infers, where it stops

figures.label: Placements
figures.caption: Ways scholars have dated the patriarchs, shown side by side. None is chosen

figures.label: Signatures
figures.caption: No text from the period names Abraham, Isaac, Jacob or Joseph. This is the normal silence for herders, not a finding against them

figuresNote: The fourth figure needs one caution. A place-name in the list of Pharaoh Shoshenq I, about 925 BC, has been read by some as “the fort (or field) of Abram”. The reading is disputed, it is centuries after any proposed date for Abraham, and this page does not count it. [check: the current state of the Shoshenq I reading and who proposed it]

jewishFrame.head: The fathers, in Jewish terms first
jewishFrame.body: In Jewish tradition Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are the Avot, the fathers, and Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah the Imahot, the mothers. The central prayer of the synagogue, the Amidah, opens by blessing the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, and Jewish teaching speaks of zechut avot, the merit of the fathers, remembered before God. The Christian reading comes after this and does not replace it: the New Testament calls Abraham the father of all who believe, and treats him as a real man who trusted God's promise (Romans 4; Galatians 3; Hebrews 11:8–19). Both traditions read these chapters as the story of a real family. This page tests what the ancient world can add to that reading.

spanRule.head: The span test
spanRule.body: A parallel can only help date a story if the custom it matches belonged to one period and not to others. So every record on this page carries a span: the earliest and latest centuries in which the custom or name is attested in the sources read. A short span near one proposed window is a useful clue. A span that runs across every window says the story fits the ancient Near East, and says nothing about when.
spanRule.caution: A span is drawn only as wide as the evidence the sources report. A gap in the record is not proof that a custom stopped. Spans are reported from the named scholars, not measured by this study.

placements.name: From the Bible's own numbers
placements.who: Eugene Merrill, Kingdom of Priests, who places Abraham's birth near 2166 BC [check: date and edition].
placements.how: Count back from Solomon's fourth year using 1 Kings 6:1, then add the 430 years of Exodus 12:40 and the ages in Genesis.
placements.limit: The result moves with every choice. It assumes an exodus near 1446 BC; a later exodus shifts it down. The Greek Old Testament and the Samaritan Pentateuch read Exodus 12:40 as covering Canaan and Egypt together, which roughly halves the time in Egypt and moves the patriarchs later. The numbers are Scripture's; the arithmetic is a reconstruction.

placements.name: The Middle Bronze Age
placements.who: William F. Albright and, later and on different grounds, Kenneth Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament [check: Kitchen's own window and page].
placements.how: Names, slave prices, treaty forms and the pattern of travel are said to fit the early second millennium best.
placements.limit: Several of the clues have since been found in later centuries too (see the span of each record). Albright's donkey-caravan picture of Abraham is no longer widely held.

placements.name: The Late Bronze Age
placements.who: Cyrus Gordon, who read the patriarchs against the Nuzi and Amarna world [check: Gordon's own dates and the work where he gives them].
placements.how: The Nuzi family customs, from the 15th and 14th centuries BC, are taken as the closest match.
placements.limit: It depends on the Nuzi parallels being specific to that age, which the 1970s critique disputed. It sits awkwardly with the Bible's own long numbers for the years in Egypt.

placements.name: A first-millennium setting for the writing
placements.who: Thomas L. Thompson, The Historicity of the Patriarchal Narratives (1974), and John Van Seters, Abraham in History and Tradition (1975).
placements.how: They argue that the customs and names fit later centuries as well or better, and treat the stories as written then. Both doubt that the stories record history.
placements.limit: This is a date for writing, not for people, and it rests on a judgment about genre this site does not share. It is reported here as theirs. Even on their own evidence, a late parallel does not show that an earlier one is impossible.

placementsNote: The Baptist Faith and Message fixes no date for Abraham. Baptists who hold Genesis to be true history place him in more than one century. So the page draws the first three windows as equals and does not choose. The fourth is shown because readers meet it everywhere, and it is labelled as the view of scholars who do not read these chapters as history.

kinds.name: Names and places
kinds.question: Do the people and towns have names that belong to their world?

kinds.name: Family law
kinds.question: Do the marriages, heirs and household gods match what tablets record?

kinds.name: Contracts and covenants
kinds.question: Do the bargains, oaths and purchases follow known forms?

kinds.name: Into Egypt
kinds.question: Does the Egypt of Joseph look like Egypt?

records.name: Jacob's kind of name
records.evidence: Names built like Jacob, a verb in the form “he grasps” or “he protects” with or without a god's name added, are common among the Amorite-speaking peoples in Old Babylonian and Mari texts of the 19th and 18th centuries BC. A name read as Yaqub-el is reported from that period. Kitchen also lists names of the same build in later centuries.
records.inference: The family's names are at home in the West Semitic world of the second millennium. That is what one would expect if they came from there.
records.limit: Name types of this kind do not vanish after 1600 BC, so the match fits more than one window. Kitchen argues they are most frequent early; Thompson argues the spread is too wide to date anything. Neither text names this Jacob.
records.check: [check: the attested form Yaqub-el and the text it comes from]

records.name: Grandfathers who are also towns
records.evidence: Several names in Abraham's family line match towns near Haran in northern Mesopotamia. A town Nahur appears in the Mari letters of the 18th century BC. Towns read as Sarugi (Serug) and Til-Turahi (Terah) appear in Assyrian texts of later centuries.
records.inference: Genesis places Abraham's kin around Haran, and Rebekah is found at “the city of Nahor”. The names fit that region closely. A family naming towns, or towns naming families, is well known in the region.
records.limit: Which came first, the person or the town, cannot be read from the tablets. The later attestations widen the span: they show the names belong to the area, not to a century.
records.check: [check: the Assyrian attestations of Sarugi and Til-Turahi, and their dates]

records.name: Ur of the Chaldeans
records.evidence: Ur in southern Mesopotamia was a great city long before and during the early second millennium, excavated by Leonard Woolley between 1922 and 1934. The Chaldeans (Kaldu) appear in Assyrian records from the 9th century BC onward.
records.inference: The phrase uses a people's name from a later time to tell the reader which Ur is meant, much as Genesis 14:14 names the town of Dan, which took that name only in Judges 18:29. Updating a place-name for later readers is not the same as getting it wrong.
records.limit: Some scholars, Cyrus Gordon among them, argued for a northern Ur near Haran instead [check: Gordon's article and date]. The evidence does not settle which Ur; most identify the southern city. The span here is the span of the word Chaldean, not of Ur.

records.name: Four kings from the east
records.evidence: No outside text names Amraphel, Arioch, Kedorlaomer or Tidal. Their names are of known types: Kedorlaomer like Elamite names built on Kudur-, Tidal like the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya, Arioch like a name Arriwuk reported at Mari.
records.inference: The names belong to real naming traditions of the second millennium, and an alliance of eastern kings raiding westward fits a time when such coalitions are known.
records.limit: The once-popular equation of Amraphel with Hammurabi of Babylon is now generally abandoned on linguistic grounds. A name type is not a person. Van Seters argued the chapter is late; Kitchen argued the coalition pattern fits only the early second millennium. Both are reconstructions.

records.name: A servant woman given to the husband
records.evidence: Old Assyrian marriage contracts from Kanesh (19th century BC) provide that a wife who bears no child within a set time may buy a slave woman for her husband. The Laws of Hammurabi, §146 (about 1750 BC), deal with a slave woman given to a husband by a priestess-wife, who later sets herself up as her mistress's equal: the mistress may not sell her, but may mark her and count her among the slaves again. A Nuzi marriage contract of the 15th century BC has a similar clause. A Neo-Assyrian contract of the 7th century BC has one too.
records.inference: Sarah giving Hagar, Rachel giving Bilhah and Leah giving Zilpah follow a practice the region knew for well over a thousand years. Hagar's rise in her own eyes and Sarah's harsh reply play out the very tension §146 tries to settle.
records.limit: This is the plainest case of the span test. The custom runs from the 19th to the 7th century, so it fits every window. Thompson and Van Seters pressed exactly this point. It shows the story is true to its world; it does not show when.
records.check: [check: the Kanesh contract cited, the Nuzi tablet number (Gilimninu contract), and the Neo-Assyrian contract's text number and date]

records.name: A servant as heir
records.evidence: Nuzi and Old Babylonian tablets record childless couples adopting an outsider, sometimes a servant, as heir; some add that a son born later takes first place.
records.inference: Abram's worry that Eliezer of Damascus will inherit fits that practice, and the LORD's answer, that his own son will be his heir, matches the clause about a son born later.
records.limit: Genesis does not say Eliezer was adopted. The tablet supplies a possible background, not a fact about him. Selman judges this one of the stronger parallels and still not one tied to a single century.
records.check: [check: the Nuzi adoption tablets usually cited, by text number]

records.name: “She is my sister”
records.evidence: E. A. Speiser, in his Anchor commentary on Genesis (1964), read Nuzi tablets as showing a legal status of “wife-sister”, a wife also adopted as her husband's sister, and explained the three stories by it.
records.inference: This is now the clearest example of a parallel withdrawn. Samuel Greengus and others re-read the tablets and found no such status; the documents record a brother giving a sister in marriage [check: Greengus, HUCA 46 (1975)].
records.limit: Genesis needs no Nuzi law here. It gives its own reasons: fear for his life, and that Sarah was in fact his half-sister (Genesis 20:12). The narrow span drawn is the span of the tablets Speiser used, which no longer carry his meaning.
records.check: [check: Greengus article title, volume and year]

records.name: Rachel and the household gods
records.evidence: Some Nuzi wills mention household gods passed to a chosen heir. Gordon and others argued that holding the gods gave a claim to the estate, which would explain why Rachel stole Laban's and why Laban chased so hard.
records.inference: The theft clearly mattered to Laban, and the gods were tied to his house. Beyond that, the legal reading has weakened.
records.limit: Moshe Greenberg argued that the wills do not make the gods a title-deed, and that Rachel's motive may have been religious or protective [check: Greenberg, JBL 81 (1962)]. Genesis gives no motive. The span is narrow only because the theory rested on one archive.

records.name: Who pays for the torn sheep
records.evidence: The Laws of Hammurabi, §§263–267, set a hired shepherd's duties: he repays losses from his own neglect, but where a god strikes the fold or a lion kills, he clears himself by oath and the owner bears the loss. Old Babylonian herding contracts set similar terms. J. J. Finkelstein compared one such contract directly with Jacob's words [check: Finkelstein, JAOS 88 (1968)].
records.inference: Jacob's complaint is that he bore what the usual terms would have charged to Laban: the torn animal, and theft by day or night. Read beside the contracts, his speech is a claim to have done more than custom required.
records.limit: Herding terms like these lasted for centuries, so the span is wide. The contract shows what Jacob meant; it does not date him.
records.check: [check: Finkelstein article title, volume and year]

records.name: Buying the cave at Machpelah
records.evidence: Manfred Lehmann compared the purchase with Hittite laws on land and feudal duty, and placed it in the second millennium [check: Lehmann, BASOR 129 (1953)]. Gene Tucker compared it instead with Neo-Babylonian “dialogue documents”, sale records written as an exchange of speeches, of the first millennium [check: Tucker, JBL 85 (1966)].
records.inference: Both agree on what matters for reading: the scene is a careful public sale, before witnesses at the city gate, with the price weighed out and the boundaries named, so that the land is beyond dispute.
records.limit: One scene, two parallels, a thousand years apart. The comparison shows the form of a legal sale; it cannot decide the century. The “sons of Heth” in Genesis need not be the Hittite empire of Anatolia (see confused words).

records.name: Oaths and boundary stones
records.evidence: Treaties between rulers survive from the third millennium to the seventh century BC. Kenneth Kitchen and Paul Lawrence collected them in Treaty, Law and Covenant in the Ancient Near East (2012) and grouped their forms by period.
records.inference: Abraham's and Isaac's pacts with Abimelech, and Jacob's with Laban, carry familiar parts: an oath, witnesses, a shared meal, a heap or pillar as a marker of the boundary.
records.limit: These are pacts between households, not empires, and they are short. Kitchen argues the shapes fit early; others see them as generic. Whether God's covenant with Abraham follows any treaty form is a question for Covenants and promises (26), and is not taken up here.
records.check: [check: Kitchen and Lawrence's grouping of the patriarchal pacts]

records.name: Asiatics arriving in Egypt
records.evidence: A wall painting in the tomb of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan, from the reign of Senusret II (about 1890 BC), shows a group of 37 “Asiatics” led by a chief named Abisha (or Ibsha), with donkeys, coloured woollen clothing, weapons and a lyre, arriving to trade.
records.inference: Semitic families travelling into Egypt with their goods and animals were a known sight in the early second millennium. Abram going down in famine, and Jacob's sons buying grain, fit that traffic.
records.limit: The painting shows one group at one tomb. It does not show the patriarchs, and it is often wrongly captioned as if it did. Travellers from Canaan reached Egypt in many centuries, so the record narrows nothing by itself.
records.check: [check: the count of 37 and the reading of the chief's name in Newberry's plates]

records.name: Twenty shekels of silver
records.evidence: Kitchen tabulates slave prices across two thousand years: about 20 shekels in the Old Babylonian period (the Laws of Hammurabi value a slave at a third of a mina, 20 shekels), about 30 in the 14th and 13th centuries, 50 to 60 in Assyria of the 8th and 7th, and higher under Persia [check: Kitchen's figures and page].
records.inference: Joseph's price of 20 shekels matches the early second-millennium level. The law of Moses later sets 30 shekels for a slave killed by an ox, which matches the next level. Kitchen counts this among his firmest clues.
records.limit: Prices varied by age, sex, place and market, and the tables rest on a limited number of documents. A single price is a clue, not a measurement. Critics answer that 20 is a round figure; Kitchen answers that later writers would have used later prices.
records.check: [check: whether the Hammurabi references are §§116, 214, 252 and the exact values]

records.name: Joseph's Egyptian names
records.evidence: Potiphar, Potiphera, Asenath and Zaphenath-paneah are Egyptian names. Donald Redford argued that their forms are best attested in the 7th and 6th centuries BC (A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph, 1970). Kitchen and James Hoffmeier answer that names of the same build occur earlier, and that a later writer could update spelling.
records.inference: The names are genuinely Egyptian, the priest's city On (Heliopolis) is real and important, and the scene is set in Egypt by someone who knew Egypt.
records.limit: The forms are argued in both directions by Egyptologists. A spelling can be updated in copying without changing who the person was. This page reports the debate and does not settle it.
records.check: [check: Hoffmeier's chapter on the Joseph names]

records.name: The wife who accuses
records.evidence: The Egyptian Tale of Two Brothers, on Papyrus d'Orbiney from about 1200 BC, tells of a married woman who tries to seduce her husband's younger brother, is refused, and accuses him falsely.
records.inference: The plot shape is shared. Everything else differs: the Egyptian tale moves into magic and transformation, while Genesis keeps to a household, a prison and God's presence with Joseph.
records.limit: A false accusation by a refused woman is a story found far beyond Egypt. The likeness shows a motif known in Egypt; it shows neither borrowing nor a date.
records.check: [check: Papyrus d'Orbiney's date and present location]

records.name: Seven lean years
records.evidence: Low Nile floods and famines are recorded across Egyptian history. The Famine Stela on the island of Sehel, cut in the Ptolemaic period, tells of seven years of low floods in the time of King Djoser, a thousand years and more before it was carved.
records.inference: Egypt knew the fear of a run of bad floods, and a count of seven years belonged to its own storytelling. Storing grain against famine fits an administrative state.
records.limit: The stela is far too late to witness any early event, and is itself a later story about the past. The span shows a lasting fear, not a dated famine.
records.check: [check: the Famine Stela's date and the edition used]

records.name: Forty days, seventy days, 110 years
records.evidence: Egyptian embalming took weeks; Herodotus in the 5th century BC gives seventy days for the whole process. Egyptian texts speak of 110 years as the ideal length of a life.
records.inference: Jacob embalmed over forty days and mourned seventy, and Joseph dying at 110 and placed in a coffin in Egypt, fit Egyptian custom closely. These are details an Egyptian reader would recognise.
records.limit: The customs lasted for most of Egypt's history, so they set the scene without dating it. Genesis's own numbers stand; the Egyptian ideal is background, not an explanation that replaces them.
records.check: [check: the Egyptian texts that name 110 years, and Herodotus 2.86]

records.name: Semites ruling the Delta
records.evidence: In the 17th and 16th centuries BC rulers of Asiatic origin, the Hyksos, governed northern Egypt from Avaris, in the eastern Delta, excavated by Manfred Bietak at Tell el-Dabʿa. Bietak reports houses and burials of Levantine type there from before the Hyksos rule as well.
records.inference: A Semite rising high at court, and a family settling in the eastern Delta, would fit this world. Some place Joseph under the Hyksos; others place him earlier, in the 12th Dynasty, from the Bible's longer numbers.
records.limit: No find at Avaris names Joseph or Jacob. The Hyksos were not Israel (see the claims below). Which Egyptian period Joseph belongs to depends on the placement chosen, and this page chooses none.
records.check: [check: Bietak's dating of the pre-Hyksos Levantine settlement at Tell el-Dabʿa]

records.name: The land of Goshen
records.evidence: The eastern Delta was grazing land and the usual entry for people from Canaan. Egyptian texts record border officials letting herders from the east bring their flocks in to water [check: the Papyrus Anastasi VI report and its date].
records.inference: Joseph's plan to settle shepherds apart, in grazing land near the frontier, fits both the geography and the Egyptian unease with herders that Genesis 46:34 records.
records.limit: Goshen as a name is not securely found in Egyptian sources of the period. The border report is later than most proposed dates for Jacob.
records.check: [check: whether Goshen appears in any Egyptian text and the date of the Anastasi report]

seasons.head: Same tablets. The verdict moved.
seasons.lead: The tablets did not change between 1950 and 1980. What changed was how much weight scholars put on them. Seeing that history is part of reading the evidence well.

rows.name: The tablets arrive
rows.text: The archives of Nuzi, Mari and Ugarit are dug and published. Albright, Gordon and Speiser read Genesis beside them and find custom after custom matched. Many conclude the stories preserve a real second-millennium world.

rows.name: The span is pressed
rows.text: Thompson and Van Seters show that many customs run into the first millennium, that some Nuzi readings were wrong, and argue the parallels prove nothing about date. Both go further and treat the stories as late fiction.

rows.name: Sorting the strong from the weak
rows.text: Millard and Wiseman's Essays on the Patriarchal Narratives accepts that some parallels fail and argues that others still fit the early second millennium better than later. Selman sorts the customs one by one.

rows.name: Fit, not proof
rows.text: Kitchen and Hoffmeier argue from slave prices, treaty forms and Egyptian detail. Others still read the chapters as late. The parallels are now mostly argued as evidence of fit, not proof of date.

seasons.lesson: A reader who hears “archaeology proves the patriarchs” and one who hears “archaeology disproves them” are both hearing a past decade's mood, not what the tablets can carry.

claims.claim: “Camels in Abraham's story prove it was written centuries later.”
claims.head: Late domestication in one valley is not absence everywhere.
claims.evidence: Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef found that camel bones in the copper-mining sites of the Aravah valley first appear in layers they date to the late 10th century BC, and argued this marks domestic camels' arrival in the southern Levant [check: their article, Tel Aviv 40 (2013)]. Genesis gives Abraham camels (Genesis 12:16) and sends a camel caravan for Rebekah (Genesis 24:10).
claims.inference: The study concerns one region's herds and mines. Kitchen and others point to earlier signs of camels in use elsewhere, and camels are a small part of the patriarchs' flocks in Genesis, listed among gifts and long journeys.
claims.limit: Earlier evidence for domestic camels is scattered and debated. It is possible that the word was updated by a later copyist for a pack animal; it is also possible that a wealthy man had a few camels before they were common. The evidence does not decide between these.

test.question: The earliest domestic camel bones at Timna are from about 930 BC. What does that let you say?

options.text: That nobody in the whole Near East had a tame camel before 930 BC.
options.why: The find dates camels in one place. Absence in one valley's bones is not absence everywhere.

options.text: That camels became common in the copper industry of the southern Levant around then.
options.why: This is what the excavated bones carry, and it is what the authors argued.

options.text: That Genesis 24 was written in 930 BC.
options.why: A date for animal bones is not a date for a writing, and the verse does not say camels were common.

claims.head: The name is later. Whether the people were is the question.
claims.evidence: The Philistines known from Egyptian records arrive on the southern coast of Canaan around 1175 BC, among the Sea Peoples. Genesis has Abimelech of Gerar called king of the Philistines (Genesis 26:1) and Abraham living in their land (Genesis 21:34).
claims.inference: Three readings are held. A later writer used the familiar name for whoever held that land, as with Dan and the Chaldeans. An earlier Aegean group was there before the great arrival, as Kitchen argues. Or, for those who read the chapters as late, the name dates the writing.
claims.limit: The Abimelech of Genesis lives inland at Gerar, makes treaties, and does not behave like the five-city Philistines of Judges. No outside text names an early Philistine group in that area.

test.question: Genesis 14:14 says Abram chased the kings “as far as Dan”, a town named Dan only in Judges 18. What does that suggest about the Philistine verses?

options.text: That Genesis can name places by the names later readers knew, so the Philistine verses may do the same.
options.why: Updating names for readers is a known feature of the text. It makes the first reading possible, not certain.

options.text: That Genesis is careless with names.
options.why: Naming a place so the reader can find it is the opposite of carelessness.

options.text: That the Philistines must have been in Canaan in Abraham's day.
options.why: The Dan example points the other way: it shows a later name can stand for an earlier place.

claims.claim: “The Ebla tablets name Abraham, Sodom and Gomorrah.”
claims.head: An early announcement. It did not survive checking.
claims.evidence: In the 1970s the tablets of Ebla in Syria, from the 24th century BC, were reported to contain the cities of the plain and biblical names [check: who announced it, and when]. Later readings of the same tablets by the edition's team, Alfonso Archi among them, did not confirm these identifications [check: Archi's published reply].
claims.inference: Ebla shows a large literate Syrian state centuries before any proposed date for Abraham. It is valuable for the region's languages and names. It is not a source on the patriarchs.
claims.limit: Names that sound alike in a transliteration can be read more than one way. The episode shows why a first report on new tablets should wait for the edition.

test.question: A news report says a newly read tablet mentions “Sodom”. What should you ask first?

options.text: Who read the signs, and has the published edition kept that reading?
options.why: Readings of new tablets change. A claim stands only once the edition and other specialists agree.

options.text: Whether the city was destroyed by fire.
options.why: That jumps past the question of whether the name is really there.

options.text: Nothing: a tablet is primary evidence.
options.why: The tablet is primary. A reading of it is not, until it is checked.

claims.head: An ancient guess, from Josephus reading Manetho.
claims.evidence: Josephus, in Against Apion book 1, quotes the Egyptian priest Manetho on the Hyksos and their expulsion, and identifies them with Israel's ancestors. The Hyksos were rulers of Asiatic origin who held northern Egypt for about a century and were driven out about 1550 BC.
claims.inference: Both are Semitic peoples in the eastern Delta, which is why the link was drawn. But Genesis presents Jacob's family as guests of Pharaoh, not as Egypt's rulers, and Exodus presents Israel as slaves who leave, not kings who are expelled.
claims.limit: Some scholars still see a memory of the Hyksos period behind parts of the Joseph or exodus stories. That is a reconstruction of background, not an identification of peoples, and the planned exodus study takes it up.

test.question: Avaris shows Semites living in the eastern Delta before and during Hyksos rule. What does that support?

options.text: That Semitic families settling in that region, as Genesis describes, fits what was there.
options.why: This is what the excavation carries.

options.text: That Joseph's house has been found.
options.why: Nothing at Avaris names Joseph. A fitting setting is not a found person.
Neither the site nor Genesis says this.

claims.claim: “The Nuzi tablets prove the patriarchs lived in the second millennium.”
claims.head: Some matched, some failed, and most ran long.
claims.evidence: The Nuzi archive is from the 15th and 14th centuries BC. Of its once-famous parallels, the wife-sister status has been withdrawn, the household-gods reading is disputed, and the surrogate-wife clause is found from the 19th to the 7th century.
claims.inference: Nuzi shows that family law in the ancient Near East looked like the family life in Genesis. That is worth knowing. It does not, by itself, date the patriarchs.
claims.limit: The same caution runs the other way: that a custom lasted into the first millennium does not show a story was written then.

test.question: A custom in Genesis is found in tablets from 1900 BC and from 650 BC. What can it date?

options.text: The story to 1900 BC, the earliest tablet.
options.why: The earliest tablet is only the earliest found. It does not exclude later times.

options.text: The story to 650 BC, the latest tablet.
options.why: The latest tablet does not exclude earlier times either.

options.text: Nothing: it fits the whole span.
options.why: That is the span test. A long-lived custom shows fit with the world, not a date.

stance.head: What this site holds
stance.confessionSource: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article I (the Scriptures)
stance.body: This site reads Genesis 12–50 as true history, the record of a real family through whom God began to keep his promise. The New Testament reads Abraham the same way: as the man who left home, offered Isaac and died still looking for a city (Hebrews 11:8–19), whose trust was credited to him as righteousness (Romans 4:3; Genesis 15:6). The confession does not fix his century. So the page shows the placements and does not choose.
stance.reconstruction: A date proposed by a scholar, a judgment that a name was updated, an identification of a king: each is a reconstruction around the text, reported with who made it. None is used to correct what Genesis says. Where a scholar's view rests on reading these chapters as fiction, the page says so and labels the view as theirs.
stance.silence: No text outside the Bible names the patriarchs. That is what one would expect: almost every named person in the tablets is a king, an official, a merchant with contracts, or a party to a lawsuit. A family of herders leaves its record in its own memory. The silence neither confirms nor counts against them.

confusedWords.note: A custom that fits a period is at home there. A custom that dates a story belongs only to one period. Most parallels on this page fit; few date.
Attested means found in a surviving text. A custom may have existed long before or after its attestations. A span is the attested range, not the true one.

confusedWords.word: Hittites and the sons of Heth
confusedWords.note: The Hittite empire was in Anatolia, now Turkey. The sons of Heth at Hebron in Genesis 23 are a people of Canaan. Whether they were connected to the empire is debated; the shared English word does not settle it.

Scholars use Amorite for a group of West Semitic speakers of the early second millennium and for the type of personal names they used. A name of Amorite type says something about language, not about who someone's ancestors were.
Patriarch means a father of the people, here Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in a wider sense Jacob's twelve sons. It is not a title used in the ancient texts.
Two words alike in English. Egypt beside Israel (32) tests the claim. This page does not repeat it.
Middle Bronze is an archaeological age, about 2000 to 1550 BC in the usual reckoning. The second millennium is 2000 to 1001 BC. They are not the same span.

reach: Nineteen records and five claims are set out here. They are the comparisons most often made, chosen because readers meet them; they are not every parallel ever proposed.
Every span is reported from the named scholars. This study has not counted tablets itself, and spans would widen or narrow with new finds.
No ancient text has been read here in its own language. Laws of Hammurabi are read in L. W. King's 1910 English; the rest are reported through the scholars named.
The page compares worlds. It can show that Genesis is at home in the ancient Near East. It cannot prove or disprove that a named person lived, and it does not try.
